newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ tribunal says Muriwhenua claims well founded.
newsitem.headline: NZ tribunal says Muriwhenua claims well founded.

text.p: The Waitangi Tribunal said in a report published on Wednesday that the Muriwhenua claims to land and New Zealand state assets in the far north were well founded.
The claims involve 170,000 hectares of land, most of it sold prior to 1840.
The Tribunal said Maori believed the land was in effect leased and not sold.
Among options suggested for settlement were the return of state forests and state enterprise assets, and financial compensation.
The Waitangi Tribunal says the land losses have had serious economic and social consequences for Far North Maori, and early action was needed.

The report found "clear breaches" of the Treaty of Waitangi, including protection, honourable conduct and fair process in relation to land transactions including land at Cape Reinga, Ninety Mile Beach and North Cape.
"The central issue of later crown purchases is therefore not so much the intention of Maori in transacting, but more importantly, the integrity of the Crown in buying," the report said.

"In short, the tribunal finds that the Crown failed in its primary responsibilities to fairly review the pre-treaty transactions and validation of surplus lands, and to ensure its own purchasing actions were just, fair and equal," the tribunal said in a statement.
The report itself says binding recommendations should be made in relation to crown forests and state enterprise assets "unless the parties agree otherwise".
Claimants had asked for binding recommendations on Aupouri State Forest and Stony Creek station but counsel for the government opposed that.

Later the report says the tribunal, in considering compensation for the claims, would want to take into account the impact of reparation on the rest of the community, as well as what lands were necessary to provide a reasonable economic base for the hapu.
The tribunal says it believes it may have to consider a total relief package, and cannot make binding recommendations in relation to part of a settlement.
It wants to hear further from the parties involved on settlement options, including options for areas of conservation land.

Treaty Negotiations Minister Doug Graham and Treasurer Winston Peters, whose tribal affiliations are based in the Far North, have urged the tribes involved to undertake serious negotiations with the government, warning that the return of such assets would be disastrous and could bankrupt the country.
Graham has said he believed the Muriwhenua claim was not in the same league as that of Tainui and Ngai Tahu, who have settled for $170 million each.
The report said delay was unnecessary in terms of settlement.
"Profound social and economic consequences for the hapu (sub-tribe) have resulted in physical deprivation, poverty, social dislocation and loss of status.

"These matters of consequential impacts in terms of land tenure reform and disempowerment, and the serious social and economic conditions that still prevail in Muriwhenua, underline the need for early relief," the tribunal said.
